prompt.context: Our client is a mid-size amusement park chain, with 10 parks around the U.S. serving over 10 million visitors each year. In their Richmond, VA park, it operates both a traditional thrill-ride section, as well as an animal experience. Currently, the two sections are covered under one entry ticket price. However, management is considering offering a separate ticket for only the animal experience section. They have come to us to determine if this is a good idea.
prompt.question: Should Seven Flags offer a separate ticket for only the animal experience section at its Richmond, VA park?

clarifying_info.q: What is management's financial goal or success criteria?
clarifying_info.a: Management wants a payback period less than 10 years. Payback period = investment / on-going profit.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current ticket price?
clarifying_info.a: Tickets are currently $20 and provide visitors full access to the park.

clarifying_info.q: How many visitors does the Richmond park see?
clarifying_info.a: The Richmond, VA park is an average sized park within the client's portfolio.

clarifying_info.q: How does the business model work?
clarifying_info.a: The park is a typical amusement park (think Six Flags or Busch Gardens). Visitors buy a ticket for entrance — same price for adults and children — and all rides and amusements are accessible under the one ticket price. The park also sells merchandise and food/drinks separately.

exhibits.title: Seven Flags Park Map
exhibits.shows: A map of the Seven Flags Richmond, VA park showing the layout of the traditional thrill-ride section and the animal experience section, illustrating that the two areas are currently accessed under one ticket.
exhibits.data: Two distinct zones: thrill-ride section and animal experience section

exhibits.title: Price Elasticity of Animal Only Admissions
exhibits.shows: A chart showing daily visitor volume at four different animal-only ticket price points, along with two notes: (1) cannibalization rate is 50%, and (2) the establishment is open 350 days per year.
exhibits.data: $10 → 1,300 visitors/day; $12 → 1,100 visitors/day; $14 → 700 visitors/day; $16 → 500 visitors/day; cannibalization rate 50%; open 350 days/year

framework: Incremental profit: analyze revenue changes (new ticket price, volume, cannibalization of full-park ticket sales) and cost changes (existing costs plus new capital expenditure)

Revenue drivers: new animal-only ticket price and volume, food/drink and merchandise uplift from incremental visitors, cannibalization of existing full-park ticket holders who switch to cheaper animal-only ticket
Existing costs: maintenance, animal care, labor/operations, COGS for merchandise and food
New/incremental costs: build-out of new entrance, wall separating ride and animal sections, additional parking, potentially more staff
Competitive landscape: other attractions in Richmond area — zoos, petting zoos, museums, movie theaters, state fairs, and other family-friendly recreational activities
Macro trends: changes in disposable income, weather conditions, consumer entertainment preferences
Payback period check: investment divided by incremental annual profit must be under 10 years per management's requirement

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, which price point for the animal-only ticket maximizes incremental revenue, and what is the yearly incremental ticket revenue at that price?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute incremental daily revenue at each price point, accounting for (a) new ticket revenue from net-new visitors and (b) revenue lost from existing full-park ticket holders who cannibalize down to the cheaper animal-only ticket. The $16 price point maximizes yearly incremental ticket revenue at approximately $1,050,000, roughly a 5% increase on current $20M ticket revenue. Strong candidates note that incremental revenue is highly sensitive to the cannibalization rate assumption.

math.setup: For each price P with daily visitor count V, cannibalization rate C=50%: New tickets sold = V*(1-C); New ticket revenue/day = P * V*(1-C); Cannibalized visitors = V*C; Revenue change per cannibalized visitor = P - $20 (negative); Daily cannibalized revenue impact = (P-$20) * V*C; Daily incremental revenue = new ticket revenue + cannibalized revenue impact; Yearly incremental revenue = daily incremental revenue * 350 days. Current baseline: ~1,000,000 visitors/year * $20 = $20,000,000 ticket revenue.
steps: $10: new tickets=650, new rev/day=$6,500; cannibalized=650, rev impact/day=($10-$20)*650=-$6,500; daily incremental=$0; yearly=$0
$12: new tickets=550, new rev/day=$6,600; cannibalized=550, rev impact/day=($12-$20)*550=-$4,400; daily incremental=$2,200; yearly=$770,000
$14: new tickets=350, new rev/day=$4,900; cannibalized=350, rev impact/day=($14-$20)*350=-$2,100; daily incremental=$2,800; yearly=$980,000
$16: new tickets=250, new rev/day=$4,000; cannibalized=250, rev impact/day=($16-$20)*250=-$1,000; daily incremental=$3,000; yearly=$1,050,000
Optimal price = $16, yearly incremental ticket revenue = $1,050,000 (~5% increase on $20M baseline)
math.answer: $16 per ticket; yearly incremental ticket revenue = $1,050,000

questions.prompt: What is the payback period for this proposal at the optimal $16 price point, and does it meet management's requirement?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recall or ask for the fixed investment cost and the profit margin, then compute incremental annual profit and divide the investment by it. The result is approximately 9.5 years, just under the 10-year requirement. Great candidates proactively remember the payback period metric from their framework or the clarifying information.

math.setup: Payback period = investment / incremental annual profit. Incremental annual profit = incremental annual revenue * profit margin. Fixed investment provided when asked: $2,000,000. Profit margin: 20%.
math.answer: ~9.5 years — just under management's 10-year threshold, so the project passes the financial hurdle

brainstorming.prompt: Aside from ticket sales, what are some other considerations that will factor into the decision?

categories.name: Other revenue sources
ideas: Food and beverage sales to incremental animal-section visitors
Parking fees from incremental visitors who come only for the animal experience
Annual passes — individual or family — for the animal experience section

categories.name: Incremental costs
ideas: Build-out of a new dedicated entrance for the animal section
Construction of a wall or barrier to separate the ride area from the animal enclosure
Additional parking capacity for new visitors
Additional employees to operate the new entrance and serve higher visitor volume

categories.name: Cannibalization risk
ideas: If cannibalization rate is higher than 50%, incremental profit shrinks and payback period extends beyond 10 years
Sensitivity analysis on cannibalization is critical before committing

categories.name: Competitive landscape
ideas: Zoos and petting zoos in the Richmond area

categories.name: Macro trends
ideas: Changes in household disposable income affecting entertainment spending
Weather conditions affecting outdoor park attendance
Shifts in consumer preferences toward animal/nature experiences vs. thrill rides

recommendation: Move forward with creating an animal-only admission ticket priced at $16
At $16, incremental annual ticket revenue is ~$1,050,000, a 5% increase on the current $20M ticket revenue base
With a 20% profit margin, incremental annual profit is ~$210,000, yielding a payback period of ~9.5 years — just below management's 10-year requirement
risks: Incremental revenue and profit are highly sensitive to the cannibalization rate; if actual cannibalization exceeds 50%, profits fall and payback period exceeds 10 years
Potential opportunity cost: the $2M capital could be deployed in higher-ROI projects elsewhere in the portfolio
next_steps: Quantify the additional revenue opportunity from food, beverages, and merchandise sales to new animal-section visitors — this would reduce the payback period further
Conduct a market study on competitive attractions in Richmond to validate incremental visitor demand assumptions
Pilot the separate ticket at one park before rolling out chain-wide
